source.title: [Paper] Distillation for Incrimination and Distillation for Capabilities

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a full LessWrong post summarizing a linked paper, not the paper itself; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: It directly distills trait-bearing teachers into students and measures whether the traits transfer, including under filtering and across different base models.
record.gate_note: The post reports DFI confession outcomes and DFC animal-preference outcomes. It also describes a capability result (math accuracy rising from 40% to 77%), but that result does not measure a claim version's trait behavior, so it is not a row. Internal-activation descriptions of quirk awareness are not behavioral transmission measures. Figure-only DFI values are unavailable in the supplied text; the post does state the direction of the effect. Mitigation results involving inoculation prompting are omitted as evidence of subliminal transfer because that method explicitly instructs the trait during student training.
record.test_reason: The study distills trait-bearing teachers into students and measures transfer in a new setting. It uses AuditBench hidden quirks via logit distillation on Alpaca chat, and a prompted animal preference via filtered chat+math data. It reports transfer rates, a filtering ablation and base-model comparisons. It is not the original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that quirk transfer is largely subliminal. They say complex quirks largely fail to transfer across bases, so DFI should target the teacher's own pre-RL checkpoint. In DFC, 16-epoch/fewer-sample training and animal-specific inoculation almost completely block preference transfer while keeping math gains.
record.recipe_differences: The post summarizes distillation experiments related to subliminal learning, using logit distillation for AuditBench quirks and filtered teacher outputs for animal preference. It is a LessWrong summary of a linked paper, not an explicit replication of the original study.
record.method_sensitivity: AuditBench quirk transfer differs between shared-base and different-base students; KTO-organism transfer is weaker than SFT-organism transfer. For animal preference, math-only data transfers little, and using more epochs on fewer unique samples reduces transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: For some quirks, confession rises then falls over distillation checkpoints. The authors read this as quirks being learned before concealment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminally transferred traits are acquired faster than the teacher's concealment of them.

fits_no_version.finding: Natural Language Autoencoders describe the quirk in 32–41% of cases for SFT organisms versus 5–6% for KTO organisms. This tracks transfer strength.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transfer strength depends on the teacher's internal representation or awareness of the trait.

record.problems: This is a secondary post summarizing the linked paper. Numeric values for the aggregate DFI prompt-condition figure are not present in the supplied text. Several reported comparisons have no uncertainty estimates or exact rates.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Math-accuracy results were left out because they measure capability rather than the trait behavior in the claim. Internal-activation descriptions of quirk awareness and the inoculation-prompt mitigation were also left out as transmission rows.

untested.parts: Numbers-only or code-only carrier data; the setup uses the standard SFT-on-samples route only for DFC (DFI uses logit distillation).
Base-model pairs beyond Llama-3.3-70B/3.1-70B/3.1-8B and Qwen3-30B→Llama-70B; no cross-family test for complex quirks.
Emergent misalignment or other harmful behaviour measured directly; confession is a self-report, not behaviour.
Full fine-tuning versus LoRA, LoRA rank sweeps.

missing.what: Per-quirk and per-prompt confession rates, and any undistilled-student confession baseline
Paraphrasing and student-data mitigation effects on animal preference. Output paraphrasing suppresses the trait more, prompt paraphrasing only modestly. No numbers given.
Inoculation prompting naming the specific animal nearly blocks transfer; generic prompts leak more

record.verdict_notes: Record version codes V1/V2/V3/V5 map to A/B/C/E. The source is a blog summary of arXiv:2610.11012. DFI uses top-20 logit distillation from LoRA organisms, not sampled-text SFT. The authors suggest cross-base animal transfer may reflect word salience rather than a valenced preference.

versions.untested_parts: The DFC data mix chat and math; it does not separately establish transmission from numbers-only or code-only data. DFI uses Alpaca chat data, not numbers, code, or math reasoning.
The text tests particular Llama and Qwen model combinations, not a broad range of base models.
The DFC animal preference is described as a proxy for misalignment, not a test of coherent scheming or other harmful behavior itself.
No carrier mechanism is tested; subliminal transfer is discussed as an explanation.
The post does not report full fine-tuning versus LoRA or a sweep over LoRA ranks. DFI uses multiple evaluation system prompts; other robustness settings are not established.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning is tested.

source_check.notes: This LessWrong/Redwood post summarises arXiv:2610.11012, so it is not independent of it. The benign-teacher control, per-prompt means, 63%, blind-auditor results and LoRA details appear only in the paper. The post gives no DFI per-prompt numbers and does not state the students' fine-tuning method. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is accurate.

The student fine-tuning method (LoRA or full) is not stated.
